headline: New Hampshire voters head to polls as open Senate seat reshapes 2026 races
dek: Tuesday’s primary is the first major test of the campaigns competing to succeed retiring U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, with congressional and statehouse contests on the same ballot.
body: New Hampshire voters are choosing nominees Tuesday in a primary that will set the field for an open U.S. Senate seat, two congressional contests, the governor’s race and the state Legislature.

The Senate contest has drawn particular attention because Jeanne Shaheen is not seeking reelection. On the Democratic side, U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas is facing a challenge from Karishma Manzur. The Republican field includes former U.S. senators John E. Sununu and Scott Brown.

The ballot also includes a crowded contest for Pappas’s current House seat in the 1st Congressional District. The general election is expected to make New Hampshire one of the country’s closely watched Senate battlegrounds.

The results will provide the first clear measure of which messages, coalitions and candidates have the strongest footing before November. NorthEast News will update this story as results are reported and verified.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: The New Hampshire Senate primary is the race to watch
dek: With Shaheen’s retirement opening a rare statewide contest, both parties are testing messages that could define the fall campaign.
body: New Hampshire’s open Senate race is drawing national attention because the state’s primary could shape one of the most competitive seats on the 2026 map.

Reuters reported that Chris Pappas entered the Democratic primary with a fundraising advantage, while Karishma Manzur has sought to close the gap with a more progressive platform and a grassroots campaign.

On the Republican side, John E. Sununu and Scott Brown bring different kinds of statewide experience to the contest. The eventual nominees will face a general election audience focused on affordability, the direction of Washington and the state’s independent political identity.
Primary results are only an opening signal, not a forecast. The electorate, issues and alliances can change substantially between September and November.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Today’s NH primary: the races and stakes on the ballot
dek: Voters are selecting nominees for Congress, governor and the Legislature in one of the state’s most consequential primary days in years.
body: The New Hampshire primary is placing nominations for Congress, governor and the 424-seat state Legislature before voters Tuesday, according to an Associated Press overview of the election.

The open Senate contest is the top-of-ticket race after Jeanne Shaheen’s decision not to seek reelection. Chris Pappas and Karishma Manzur are competing for the Democratic nomination, while John E. Sununu and Scott Brown are among the Republicans seeking their party’s nomination.

Voters are also selecting candidates for the state’s two U.S. House districts. The results will determine which candidates advance to the November general election and will give campaigns a clearer sense of the issues resonating with primary voters.
This is a guide to the major contests, not a projection. NorthEast News will add verified results and candidate statements as they become available.

headline: Boston Scientific says cyberattack could hit its 2026 outlook
dek: The Marlborough-based medical-device maker said an August incident disrupted parts of its global operations and made its prior forecast harder to meet.
body: Boston Scientific said Tuesday that it is unlikely to meet previously issued third-quarter and full-year 2026 sales and adjusted-profit forecasts after a cyberattack disrupted global operations.

Reuters reported that the unauthorized activity was identified August 25 and caused network outages that affected manufacturing and order processing. The company said major distribution and manufacturing operations have resumed, while the full financial impact remains uncertain.
The company had previously forecast 2026 adjusted earnings of $3.28 to $3.32 per share and sales growth of 5.5% to 6.5%. It plans to provide an updated outlook with third-quarter results in October.
The incident is a reminder that cybersecurity risk can move quickly from an information-technology problem into a supply-chain and earnings issue for Massachusetts manufacturers.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Providence housing fight puts affordability at the center of the mayoral primary
dek: The city’s debate over rent control, zoning and new construction is giving Rhode Island voters a local test of a national housing dilemma.
body: Housing affordability has become the central issue in Providence’s mayoral primary, where candidates are offering different answers to rising rents and a shortage of new construction.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Mayor Brett Smiley is emphasizing additional housing production and zoning changes, while state Rep. David Morales is arguing for rent control as a way to offer more immediate relief to current renters.

The disagreement reflects a familiar policy tension: measures intended to protect tenants today can affect the incentives developers face when deciding whether to build tomorrow. Both sides are presenting their approach as a response to the same pressure on household budgets.
The result will offer an early indication of how Providence voters weigh short-term protections against longer-term supply and development strategies.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Qualcomm and Amazon deepen AI-chip ties in multibillion-dollar agreement
dek: The deal expands Amazon’s custom-chip push and gives Qualcomm another foothold in the infrastructure behind AI services.
body: Qualcomm and Amazon announced an agreement Tuesday centered on AI data-center chips and high-speed optical connectivity, adding another major partnership to the race to build AI infrastructure.
Reuters reported that Amazon will purchase Qualcomm’s AI data-center products and that Qualcomm granted Amazon warrants valued at about $4 billion. Qualcomm shares rose after the announcement.
The companies said they will work on inference chips and connectivity technology. The arrangement also calls for Qualcomm to expand its use of Amazon Web Services while accelerating chip-design work.
The partnership illustrates how cloud companies are building more of their own silicon while chip designers look beyond smartphones for growth.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Mistral raises record funding round as the AI race accelerates
dek: The French AI company’s €3 billion raise values it at roughly €21 billion and adds another data point to the global infrastructure and model-building boom.
body: French AI company Mistral has raised €3 billion in a funding round that values the three-year-old company at roughly €21 billion, according to Reuters.
The round was led by PSG Equity and included Samsung Electronics and the EU-backed Scaleup Europe Fund. Mistral plans to use the money to expand its AI models, research and cloud offerings.

The deal makes Mistral one of Europe’s most valuable private technology companies as governments and investors push for more domestic alternatives in a market dominated by U.S. and Chinese competitors.
For New England readers, the funding is another signal that demand for engineers, data-center capacity and AI services is likely to remain a major force across the technology economy.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Wall Street slips as oil climbs and geopolitical risk rises
dek: Stocks pulled back Tuesday as higher energy prices and bond yields renewed inflation concerns ahead of a closely watched U.S. data release.
body: U.S. stocks declined Tuesday as a jump in oil prices and higher bond yields added to investor concerns about inflation and the outlook for interest rates.

Reuters reported that the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.21%, the S&P 500 lost 0.49% and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.52%. Brent crude reached $98.28 per barrel while U.S. crude reached $93.40.
The market was also watching a stronger yen and a rise in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield. Investors are looking ahead to inflation data due Friday for clues about the Federal Reserve’s next move.
These are reported market figures, not a live quote feed. NorthEast News will connect a delayed or real-time data provider separately before presenting market numbers as a product feature.

headline: Record copper prices show the material cost of the AI boom
dek: Demand from data centers, electrical grids and electric vehicles is colliding with supply constraints and trade-policy uncertainty.
body: Copper prices reached a record Tuesday as demand from AI data centers and other power-intensive industries met concerns about supply and possible tariffs.

Barron’s reported that New York front-month copper futures rose 2.8% to $6.78 per pound, surpassing the previous record. Mining shares also advanced as investors priced in the possibility of sustained demand.

Copper is a useful marker for the physical buildout behind digital services. Data centers, transmission upgrades and electric vehicles all require substantial amounts of the metal, even as miners face long development timelines.
The move is a reminder that the AI economy is not only a software story. Materials, electricity, construction and regional infrastructure are part of the same investment cycle.
author: NorthEast News Desk

headline: Massachusetts mistrial keeps postpartum-psychosis debate in view
dek: A judge declared a mistrial after jurors deadlocked in the case, while the defense argued that severe mental illness should shape how responsibility is understood.
body: A Massachusetts case ended in a mistrial after jurors could not reach a verdict, leaving a high-profile debate over postpartum psychosis and criminal responsibility unresolved.

The Guardian reported that the defense argued the defendant was experiencing postpartum psychosis at the time of the deaths of her three children. Expert testimony presented during the trial addressed the role of severe mental illness.
A mistrial is not an acquittal or a conviction. The court’s decision means the case remains unresolved and any next steps will depend on the prosecution and the court.

The case has renewed discussion about maternal mental-health treatment, crisis support and how courts evaluate psychiatric evidence. This summary avoids graphic detail while the legal process continues.

headline: New Hampshire businesses build community around alcohol-free drinks
dek: Concord and Manchester businesses are adding nonalcoholic drinks and social spaces as more customers look for alternatives to traditional bars.
body: New Hampshire businesses are responding to growing interest in alcohol-free drinks, with cafes, restaurants and social venues creating places where people can gather without ordering alcohol.

NHPR reported that Gnomies, a cafe, dry bar, board-game lounge and art-class venue, opened in Concord this summer. In Manchester, the family-run Rumi Kabob House has also made nonalcoholic drinks part of its social atmosphere.

The shift is arriving as alcohol consumption declines and customers look for more choices. For small businesses, the trend is both a hospitality change and a practical experiment in how to build repeat traffic around conversation, food and activities rather than alcohol sales.

For operators, the model can also open daytime and family-friendly business hours. The broader question is whether alcohol-free menus become a permanent part of New Hampshire hospitality or remain a niche for customers taking a break from drinking.
That gives communities another kind of gathering place while giving owners a way to serve customers who want a social night out without the usual bar setting.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Concord farm meets high local demand for greens after lettuce recalls
dek: A two-person farm says it has been selling out weekly as shoppers and restaurants put a premium on local lettuce and microgreens.
body: Generation Farm in Concord has been selling out of greens each week this summer, according to New Hampshire Public Radio, as local growers respond to strong demand from restaurants, co-ops and other buyers.

James and Marley Stever run the farm themselves, growing lettuce in outdoor beds and microgreens inside a barn with grow lights. The small operation is handling production, customer service and deliveries with no larger staff behind it.

The farm’s busy season comes after cyclospora-related lettuce recalls, including a recall affecting New Hampshire, pushed some consumers to reconsider where their produce comes from. The experience shows how a food-safety concern can quickly reshape demand for nearby farms.

Local farms cannot replace every large-volume supplier, but the Concord example shows why direct relationships matter. Restaurants and shoppers get a clearer connection to the source, while growers gain a chance to turn a short-term concern into lasting demand for regional food.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: UMass Boston chancellor plans to step down in February
dek: Marcelo Suárez-Orozco will leave the post after seven years, closing a tenure that included campus growth and a major capital overhaul.
body: UMass Boston Chancellor Marcelo Suárez-Orozco plans to step down Feb. 1 after seven years leading the university, WBUR reported. He took the job as the COVID-19 pandemic began reshaping higher education.

Suárez-Orozco, who is nearing 70, said he wants to make room for the next generation of university leaders. He also plans to refocus on climate-resilience work and the ethical use of technology, including artificial intelligence.

During his tenure, UMass Boston rose in national research-university rankings and earned top-tier research status from the Carnegie Foundation in 2025. The campus also moved through a long-delayed $293 million overhaul of facilities first opened in 1974.

The coming leadership transition will arrive as universities balance research ambitions, capital needs and pressure to show students a clear return on the cost of attendance. UMass Boston has not yet announced a successor in the report.
The university will now face the familiar challenge of preserving that momentum while choosing a leader for its next chapter.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Eastern Massachusetts seeks more Quabbin water as review begins
dek: A request for up to 20 million additional gallons a day is prompting questions about which communities need the supply and what alternatives were considered.
body: Eastern Massachusetts officials are seeking as much as 20 million more gallons of water each day from the Quabbin Reservoir, a proposal that is now moving through the state’s interbasin-transfer review process.

The Quabbin is a primary source for the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority system and supplies drinking water to roughly 2.7 million people. State law requires an application to explain which communities will receive the water, why it is needed and whether other options were examined.

New England Public Media reported that state Rep. Aaron Saunders questioned whether those answers are fully spelled out in the current application. The review places long-term growth, water demand and reservoir protection in the same public debate.

The reservoir covers roughly 39 square miles and is protected as an unfiltered drinking-water source. Any decision will therefore involve more than capacity: it will also require officials to explain how additional withdrawals fit with conservation and watershed protections.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Rhode Island governor primary rematch centers on bridge and trust
dek: Incumbent Dan McKee and Helena Foulkes are facing each other again, with the Washington Bridge crisis and state leadership at the center of the contest.
body: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee and Helena Foulkes are meeting again in a Democratic primary, four years after McKee narrowly defeated Foulkes. The rematch is unfolding as voters continue to weigh the state’s handling of the Washington Bridge repairs.

Foulkes, a former CVS Health executive, has outraised McKee and put significant advertising behind her challenge, according to The Associated Press. McKee is defending his record and emphasizing labor support as he seeks another term.

The bridge’s partial closure, delays and cost concerns have become a central test of public confidence. The primary is scheduled for Wednesday, Sept. 9, and the result could set the direction of Rhode Island’s next statewide campaign.

The race is also a test of whether voters treat infrastructure management as a defining leadership issue. Both campaigns are asking Democrats to view the state’s recent problems through a different lens: competence and continuity for McKee, or change for Foulkes.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: What Rhode Island voters should know before Wednesday’s primary
dek: The state’s Sept. 9 primary will release results through 39 local jurisdictions, with early and mail ballots mixed into the night’s reporting.
body: Rhode Island’s primary election is Wednesday, Sept. 9, after the state moved the contest away from the day after Labor Day to give cities and towns more time to prepare polling places.

The Associated Press said Rhode Island’s 39 jurisdictions are expected to release results throughout the evening. Early in-person and mail ballots are not necessarily reported at the beginning of the night, so the first numbers may not show the full shape of the vote.

The Democratic governor’s race between Dan McKee and Helena Foulkes is the top statewide contest. The state also has congressional and legislative nominations on the ballot, with unaffiliated voters making up the largest registration group.

That reporting structure means a close race may remain unsettled after the first wave of returns. Voters looking for a quick result should watch the release schedule and remember that local totals can arrive at different speeds.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: New Hampshire school-ID voting rule gets first test at UNH
dek: A new identification rule was challenged in federal court but appeared to create few problems for Durham voters during Tuesday’s primary.
body: A new New Hampshire law removing school-issued IDs from the approved identification list got its first major test Tuesday at the University of New Hampshire’s Durham polling place.

NHPR reported that the law, signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte this summer, is being challenged in federal court. At Oyster River High School, voters were advised that a school ID alone would not be accepted for registration or obtaining a ballot.

One UNH student told NHPR she registered with a driver’s license and a utility bill and found the process easy. Durham’s town moderator said operations were running smoothly and turnout was steady, though voting-rights groups continued warning students about the change.

The Durham experience does not resolve the legal challenge or answer how the policy will work in every community. It does show how election workers and campus groups are adapting in real time as college students arrive with questions about acceptable documents.

headline: Springfield public schools close after cyber incident
dek: All public schools and after-school activities were canceled Tuesday while officials investigated an incident affecting systems used for essential operations.
body: All public schools in Springfield, Massachusetts, were closed Tuesday after a cyber incident interrupted systems needed for essential school operations, New England Public Media reported.

The district also canceled after-school activities and directed staff to stay off district network systems. Students with district-issued laptops were told to do the same while officials worked to determine what happened.

The incident’s scope remained under investigation. The district’s Central Office stayed open, although officials warned that some services, including phone lines, could be affected. The closure was described as a step to give technology and school leaders time to address the disruption.

Officials had not publicly identified the cause, the systems affected or a timetable for full restoration in the report. Those details will determine whether the closure remains a one-day response or expands into a larger operational problem.
School officials said the closure was intended to protect essential operations while the district worked through the immediate response.
