headline: South Station’s high-tech fare gates hit a weather problem
dek: Nearly half the commuter-rail gates were covered during a recent rainy morning, limiting ticket scanning at Boston’s busiest station.
body: The MBTA’s new high-tech fare gates at South Station are designed to scan commuter-rail passes, tickets and phones before passengers board and again when they arrive. The project cost $3.5 million and was intended to improve fare collection.

But WBUR found 19 of the station’s 40 gates covered by tarps during a recent rainy weekday morning. The covered gates meant passengers using tracks 8 through 13 could not scan tickets in the normal way.

Keolis said it first noticed the weather-related problem early this year and that gates on part of the concourse have been covered about 10% of the time since February. The issue adds a basic durability question to a technology project aimed at making transit more efficient.

South Station handles about 110,000 passengers a day, making even a partial gate shutdown visible to commuters. The episode also highlights the gap between installing new equipment and testing how it performs under the weather conditions Boston riders regularly face.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Massachusetts data centers face local approval before state permits
dek: Gov. Maura Healey’s new order requires community agreements and bars state-agency nondisclosure deals with proposed facilities.
body: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey signed an executive order Tuesday requiring proposed data-center projects to receive local approval before developers can move into state permitting, WBUR reported.

Pending projects must negotiate community-benefits agreements that meet state standards with their host communities. The order also blocks nondisclosure agreements between state agencies and data-center developers, which Healey’s office said would make the process more transparent.

The policy is the latest step in the state’s effort to set conditions around facilities that can bring jobs and investment but also require substantial electricity, water and land. Massachusetts halted tax breaks for data centers earlier this summer.

Local approval requirements could give cities and towns more leverage over noise, traffic, utility demand and economic benefits before a project reaches the state level. The order makes those local negotiations an early gate in the development process.
The approach could become a model for how other states balance local control with demand for computing capacity.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Biotech shares slide after Novartis muscle-disease trial setback
dek: Dyne, Sarepta and PepGen fell after a late-stage Novartis drug failed to show a statistically significant benefit in a muscle-disease trial.
body: Shares of several biotech companies fell Tuesday after Novartis said a late-stage study of its drug del-desiran failed to show a statistically significant improvement in a measure of hand function for people with myotonic dystrophy type 1.

Reuters reported that Dyne Therapeutics led the decline, dropping 18%, while Sarepta and PepGen also fell more than 9% and 5%, respectively. Novartis shares were down nearly 11% in the reported session.

The result matters beyond one drug because the companies are pursuing related approaches to rare muscle diseases. Analysts were still assessing whether the setback reflected the treatment mechanism, the trial design or both. These are reported market moves, not live quotes.

Novartis acquired the program through its purchase of Avidity, adding a deal-making angle to the market reaction. Investors are now watching whether other companies’ trial data can separate a single-study failure from a broader problem for the field.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Software stocks fall as investors weigh the next AI disruption
dek: Salesforce, Intuit and ServiceNow were among the software names under pressure as investors turned to inflation data and the pace of AI adoption.
body: U.S. stocks moved lower Tuesday as software shares came under pressure from renewed concerns that artificial intelligence could disrupt established software businesses, Reuters reported.

The S&P 500 fell 0.58% to 7,673.52 in the reported session, while Salesforce, Intuit and ServiceNow each declined between 4% and 5%. The S&P software and services index fell 1.4% for a second straight day.

Investors were also watching the next inflation report and the possibility that interest-rate expectations could change. Semiconductor shares were stronger after Qualcomm’s new Amazon partnership, showing how the same AI trend can weigh on software companies while supporting chip demand. Figures are reported, not live quotes.

The split illustrates how markets are sorting winners and losers inside the AI trade rather than treating technology as one category. Companies selling infrastructure may benefit from spending while firms worried about software substitution face a different question about future pricing power.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Patriots’ Christian Gonzalez agrees to record cornerback contract
dek: The four-year, $135 million deal would make Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history, according to people who spoke with the AP.
body: New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez has agreed to a four-year, $135 million contract, a deal that would make him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history, The Associated Press reported.
Two people with knowledge of the agreement told the AP that $102 million is guaranteed. They spoke anonymously because the team had not yet announced the contract publicly.

The agreement gives Gonzalez the long-term security he had been seeking after emerging as a central part of the Patriots’ defense. For New England, it is also a major commitment to a young player before the season’s competitive stakes fully arrive.

The contract reflects how quickly elite young defensive players can reset the market at a premium position. It also gives the Patriots a clear signal of how they value Gonzalez as the team builds around a core of long-term contributors.
The team’s eventual announcement will establish the final terms.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Neighbors and firefighters rescue 17-year-old dog in Dorchester
dek: Milly, who is blind and deaf, wandered from her fenced yard before a neighborhood search brought her safely home about four hours later.
body: A neighborhood search in Dorchester ended with the safe return of Milly, a 17-year-old dog who is blind and deaf and had wandered away from her fenced-in yard, WBUR reported.

Milly’s family realized the gate might not have latched and began looking through Ashmont Hill. Neighbors joined the search, and firefighters from the Engine 18/Ladder 6 house helped locate the dog after she had spent roughly four hours moving around the neighborhood.
The rescue brought Milly back to her family and offered a small reminder of how quickly a local search can become a community effort. Firefighters even used steak to help coax the dog to safety.

For the family, the happy ending came after an anxious afternoon and a search that crossed the ordinary boundaries of one household. The story also shows the practical value of neighbors sharing information quickly when a vulnerable animal goes missing.

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A 24-year-old Manchester woman was arrested after a Monday evening crash that seriously injured a 1-year-old child, according to Manchester police information reported by Boston 25 News.

Police said officers responded around 6 p.m. to the intersection of Hanover and Belmont streets for a two-vehicle crash. They said Brianne Gonzalez was driving a 2003 Toyota RAV4 and was ejected from the vehicle; she was taken to a hospital.

Three passengers were in the RAV4, including two women and the child. Police said the child was airlifted to Boston Children’s Hospital with serious injuries, while the two women suffered minor injuries. The driver of the second vehicle, a 49-year-old Manchester man, was also taken to a hospital; police did not release his condition.

Gonzalez was charged with aggravated driving under the influence and endangering the welfare of a child. Boston 25 reported that she remained hospitalized. The investigation is continuing, and authorities asked anyone with information to contact Manchester police.
dek: Police say a two-vehicle crash in Manchester sent a child to Boston Children’s Hospital and led to aggravated OUI and child-endangerment charges.
headline: Manchester woman charged after crash seriously injures 1-year-old

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Canada imposed tariffs Tuesday on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods after the latest escalation in the trade dispute with Washington, according to an Associated Press report carried by New Hampshire Public Radio.

The measures cover hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment. Canadian officials said the tariffs match U.S. measures dollar for dollar and rate for rate, taking effect at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday.

The immediate national impact may be limited, but RBC Economics said some businesses could be hit hard. The dispute matters in New Hampshire because manufacturers, retailers, farmers and tourism operators all operate in a region where cross-border commerce and Canadian visitors are part of the economic picture.

The AP reported that the two countries’ supply chains remain deeply integrated and that Washington has threatened additional tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel next year. The next round of negotiations will determine whether Tuesday’s action remains a pressure tactic or becomes a longer disruption.
dek: Ottawa imposed tariffs on about $20 billion in U.S. goods Tuesday, adding fresh uncertainty for a New Hampshire economy tied to its northern neighbor.
headline: Canada’s new tariffs put New Hampshire trade links in focus
sourceName: New Hampshire Public Radio / Associated Press

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: About 46,000 Boston Public Schools students returned to classrooms Tuesday, with Mayor Michelle Wu and Superintendent Mary Skipper welcoming families at Holland Elementary, Boston 25 News reported.

The school year begins with the elementary school fully under district control after Boston exited state receivership. District leaders are also watching transportation closely as hundreds of buses resume daily service across the city.

Boston Public Schools is using GPS tracking through its Zoom system to monitor buses and student transportation. Skipper said the district is aiming for a 95% on-time bus success rate as routes settle into the new year.

The district also said about 15,000 students took part in summer learning programs. For families, the first days of school will provide the clearest test of whether the transportation changes and operational planning translate into reliable arrival and dismissal times.
The opening-day rollout also gives families a near-term measure of how well the district’s transportation technology and staffing plans are working.
dek: Boston Public Schools welcomed students Tuesday as the district began a new year with a fully district-run elementary school and a renewed focus on bus reliability.
headline: 46,000 Boston students return as schools start new year

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts is building a new government response to extreme heat, a hazard that can strain public health, schools and workplaces even when it leaves little visible damage, Axios reported Tuesday.

The state announced in August that it had become the first on the East Coast to appoint a heat resilience officer, following Arizona. The role reflects a broader shift as states write heat plans, add worker protections and invest in cooling infrastructure.

Axios reported that Massachusetts’ early goals include reducing heat-related school closures, improving workplace safety and expanding urban greenery. Those efforts put more emphasis on preparation before dangerous conditions arrive, rather than treating heat only as a weather forecast.

The policy question is how the state will turn a new position into measurable local support. That could include coordination with cities, employers, public-health agencies and schools as hotter periods become a more regular planning concern.
It also raises practical questions about who receives warnings, cooling help and workplace guidance when temperatures become dangerous.
dek: The state is among the first to build a dedicated government response around a hazard that often causes serious health risks without obvious property damage.
headline: Massachusetts’ new heat-resilience role puts extreme heat on state agenda

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Providence voters are weighing sharply different housing strategies in Wednesday’s Democratic mayoral primary, where affordability has become the central issue, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Incumbent Mayor Brett Smiley is emphasizing new housing construction and growth. State Rep. David Morales, his challenger, is advocating rent control as a more immediate response for tenants facing high rents.

The argument reflects a tension familiar across New England: additional supply may take years to affect prices, while stronger rent protections can change the economics developers consider when deciding whether to build. Both campaigns are presenting their approach as a response to the same shortage and cost pressure.

The primary will give Providence voters a direct choice over whether city government should prioritize faster production, stronger tenant protections or a combination of both. The result could shape the city’s housing debate and influence the November campaign.
That debate is especially consequential in a city where housing policy is a daily cost-of-living issue rather than an abstract planning question.
dek: Mayor Brett Smiley and state Rep. David Morales are offering competing answers to the city’s affordability crisis ahead of Wednesday’s Democratic primary.
headline: Providence mayoral primary turns on rent control and housing growth

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island’s Wednesday primary will decide more than the closely watched Democratic governor’s contest between Dan McKee and Helena Foulkes, the Associated Press reported.

The ballot includes contested nominations for U.S. Senate, U.S. House, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, the state Senate, the state House and Providence mayor. Polls close at 8 p.m. Eastern, and unaffiliated voters may choose either party’s primary.

About 359,000 of the state’s roughly 695,000 active registered voters were unaffiliated as of Sept. 1, according to AP. The share makes participation by independent voters an important variable in both statewide and local races.

The AP also reported that early and mail votes are mixed into results from Rhode Island’s 39 cities and towns rather than released in one front-loaded batch. That means the first returns may not show the full shape of a close contest.
Those counting rules make patience and careful reading of updates especially important on election night.
dek: Wednesday’s contest includes federal, state and local nominations, with Providence’s mayoral race and a large unaffiliated electorate adding to the stakes.
headline: Rhode Island primary tests more than the governor’s race

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Everett City Hall closed Tuesday after the city announced a cybersecurity incident affecting its internal network and technology systems, Boston 25 News reported.

City officials said Everett police, the fire department, the Department of Public Works, public schools and libraries would operate as normal. Online bill payments and third-party online transactions were not affected, according to the report.

The city did not publicly identify the cause, the systems involved or whether information was accessed. Everett officials said they were continuing to assess the incident and share updates as details emerged.

The closure is a developing municipal disruption rather than a declaration about the incident’s ultimate scope. Residents should rely on city updates for service changes while officials work to restore normal City Hall operations and determine what protections are needed.
Municipal cyber incidents can affect routine services even when emergency response and public-facing operations continue, making clear status updates important for residents.
dek: The city said its internal network and technology systems were affected Tuesday, while police, fire, schools, libraries and online payments continued operating.
headline: Everett City Hall closes after cybersecurity incident

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A large car fire stalled afternoon traffic on Interstate 95 South near Exit 18 in Foxborough Tuesday, Boston 25 News reported.

The station said the fire call came in around 1:31 p.m. and that the right and middle southbound lanes were closed as crews responded. The report did not immediately identify the vehicle or say what caused the fire.

Traffic conditions were changing while emergency crews worked in the area. Drivers approaching the Foxborough stretch of I-95 should allow extra time and follow directions from police and transportation officials.
The incident remained developing at the time of publication. Additional information about injuries, the vehicle and the reopening of the lanes was not immediately available in the initial report.
Boston 25 said the cause was not immediately clear and did not report whether anyone was injured in the initial traffic alert.
Motorists should check current traffic information before using the route because lane closures and backups can change quickly.
dek: A large vehicle fire temporarily closed two southbound lanes near Exit 18 Tuesday afternoon while officials worked at the scene.
headline: Car fire stalls afternoon traffic on I-95 in Foxborough

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts officials are offering Insulet Corp. a record $40 million package in an effort to keep the medical-device company headquartered and expanding in the state, the Boston Business Journal reported through NBC Boston.

Acton-based Insulet makes automated insulin-delivery systems and has remained headquartered in Massachusetts since its founding in 2000. The company reported $2.7 billion in revenue in 2025 and a global workforce of about 5,400, according to the report.

State officials described the package as their most aggressive job-creation offer yet. The proposal highlights the competition among states to retain medical technology companies that combine manufacturing, software and high-skilled research jobs.
The outcome will show how much public support Massachusetts is willing to put behind a local medtech company and whether Insulet’s growth plans can remain tied to the state’s innovation economy.
It is also a test of whether incentives can preserve the local benefits of a growing company without separating public support from clear job and investment commitments.
dek: State officials are offering $40 million in incentives as the Acton medical-device company weighs its future footprint in the Commonwealth.
headline: Massachusetts offers record package to keep Insulet

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts will require new data centers to secure local community support before receiving state permits under an executive order announced Tuesday by Gov. Maura Healey, NBC Boston reported.

The framework calls for a community benefits agreement with the host community and bars state agencies from using nondisclosure agreements with developers. Projects must also supply their own clean energy or pay into a ratepayer protection fund.

Developers will need to show that proposed facilities will not harm water supplies or the environment and will provide community benefits such as jobs. The rules apply to new data centers, not ongoing legal disputes involving already established facilities.

The order adds a new layer to Massachusetts’ debate over AI infrastructure. Supporters point to jobs and investment, while critics are focused on electricity, water, noise and air-pollution concerns. The state has roughly 50 data centers, most in Greater Boston.
The order is designed to make those tradeoffs part of the permitting process before construction begins.
dek: Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order ties state permits for new facilities to community agreements, energy protections and environmental review.
headline: New Massachusetts data-center rules require local support and clean energy

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Oil prices rose to six-week highs Tuesday after Iran-backed Houthi forces attacked Saudi energy facilities, renewing concerns about supply disruptions in a market already strained by the wider Middle East conflict, Reuters reported.

Brent crude reached $97.92 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate settled at $93.03, according to Reuters. The report said the Houthis targeted four southern Saudi cities, with more than 70 people injured and oil installations damaged.

The developments add to pressure on fuel and transportation costs while investors assess whether disruptions could last. Higher energy prices can also reinforce inflation concerns and influence expectations for interest-rate policy.

These are reported market figures from Reuters’ current coverage, not a live quote feed. Prices can move after publication as governments, producers and traders respond to the attacks and any changes to regional shipping or exports.
For households, the key local effect would come through fuel and freight costs if the supply concerns persist.
dek: Brent crude and U.S. oil rose after attacks on Saudi facilities intensified supply concerns and added to inflation pressure for investors.
headline: Oil hits six-week high after attacks on Saudi energy sites

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: HSBC raised its year-end target for the S&P 500 to 8,100 from 7,650, citing stronger corporate earnings and continued investment in AI infrastructure, Reuters reported Tuesday.

The new target implies a potential 4.9% gain from the index’s latest close. HSBC expects earnings per share growth to accelerate in the second half of 2026, while Reuters said 86% of 492 S&P 500 companies reporting so far had exceeded analyst estimates.
The bank also listed risks, including possible Federal Reserve rate increases, geopolitical tension, the November midterm elections and the liquidity demands of new stock offerings and AI investment.

An index target is an analyst forecast, not a live market price or guarantee. Investors are still weighing whether strong earnings can offset higher energy costs, uncertain rates and the narrow valuation range in which technology stocks have been trading.
The forecast is therefore best read as a view on earnings and capital spending, not as a promise that the broad market will follow a straight line higher.
dek: The bank cited stronger corporate earnings and AI-infrastructure investment while warning that inflation, rates and geopolitics could still unsettle markets.
headline: HSBC raises S&P 500 year-end target to 8,100

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Topsfield Fair is warning vendors about scam emails that appear to be connected to the event, Boston 25 News reported Tuesday.

Organizers urged vendors to be cautious with messages from scammers and to verify requests through official fair contacts before sending money, account details or other sensitive information. The initial report did not identify a confirmed loss or disclose how many vendors were targeted.

The warning arrives as fairs and seasonal events exchange large volumes of applications, invoices and logistics messages. That makes familiar names and deadlines useful cover for phishing attempts, especially when a request pressures a recipient to act quickly.

Vendors should avoid clicking unexpected links, confirm payment instructions independently and report suspicious messages to the fair or the relevant email provider. The fair’s warning is a reminder that local events are also targets for routine online fraud.
The fair’s message did not identify a confirmed loss, so vendors should treat the warning as prevention rather than evidence of a broader breach.
dek: Fair organizers say vendors should be cautious about messages that appear to come from the event and request sensitive information or payments.
headline: Topsfield Fair warns vendors about scam emails

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Stanley Cup is coming to Stoughton High School on Thursday after Carolina Hurricanes equipment manager Jorge Alves arranged a visit to his former school, Boston 25 News reported.

Alves graduated from Stoughton High School in 1997. The Carolina Hurricanes won the 2026 Stanley Cup, and NHL tradition gives members of the championship team an opportunity to spend a day with the trophy.
The school said Alves will bring the Cup to Stoughton from 2:30 to 4:15 p.m. Thursday. The event is free and open to the public, according to the report.
The visit gives a local connection to the Hurricanes’ championship season and turns a familiar school gym or campus setting into a celebration of a Stoughton graduate’s role behind the team.
The trophy visit is expected to draw students, alumni and local hockey fans who want to see one of sports’ most recognizable prizes in person.
School officials said the public will be able to attend during the scheduled afternoon window.
dek: Carolina Hurricanes equipment manager Jorge Alves, a 1997 Stoughton graduate, will bring the championship trophy to his former school.
headline: Stanley Cup coming to Stoughton High School Thursday

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas won New Hampshire’s Democratic primary for U.S. Senate on Tuesday night, setting up the next phase of a closely watched contest for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.

New Hampshire Public Radio reported that Pappas led Karishma Manzur with 62% of the vote as of 8:20 p.m., with 27% of ballots counted. The tally was still incomplete, but the outlet reported that voters had selected Pappas as the Democratic nominee.

Pappas has represented the state’s 1st Congressional District since 2019. His move into the Senate race also leaves an open House seat, adding another competitive contest to New Hampshire’s November ballot.

The general election is expected to draw national money and attention because control of the Senate could turn on a small number of open or closely divided seats. The early primary count is not a final certified result; local election officials and the secretary of state will complete the canvass before totals become official.
dek: The three-term congressman advances to a nationally watched general-election contest for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
headline: Chris Pappas wins New Hampshire Democratic Senate primary

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu won New Hampshire’s Republican Senate primary Tuesday, earning a place in the November race for the seat Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is leaving after three terms.

New Hampshire Public Radio reported that Sununu had 70% of the vote to Scott Brown’s 25% as of 8:20 p.m., with 16% counted. The figures were preliminary, but NHPR reported that Republican voters had selected Sununu as their nominee.

Sununu previously represented New Hampshire in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 and served one term in the U.S. House before that. Brown, a former Massachusetts senator, had also sought a New Hampshire Senate seat in 2014.

Sununu will face Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who won his party’s primary Tuesday. The matchup gives voters a choice between two candidates with federal experience and puts New Hampshire at the center of the national fight for Senate control. Final totals remain subject to the state’s official canvass.
dek: The former senator defeated Scott Brown and will face Democrat Chris Pappas for New Hampshire’s open U.S. Senate seat.
headline: John E. Sununu wins New Hampshire Republican Senate primary

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Springfield Public Schools will remain closed Wednesday as the western Massachusetts district works to contain and assess a cyberattack that disrupted key systems and forced Tuesday’s shutdown.

Mayor Domenic Sarno described the incident as a severe, “level 4” attack, according to reporting by NEPM and New Hampshire Public Radio. Officials said malicious traffic was first detected Sept. 1, and families were notified later in the week as investigators worked to understand the scope.

The district said it cannot currently access student health records or the information used to manage transportation and food service. School email is also unavailable, so administrators are relying on text messages and social media for public updates. Students and families have been told not to use school-issued laptops while technicians check for the risk of malware spreading.

City government systems were not affected, officials said. The extended closure is a meaningful escalation from the initial one-day disruption, and leaders warned that schools could remain closed longer. The district has not publicly attributed the attack or given a timetable for restoring full service.
dek: The district will remain shut Wednesday as officials work without access to student health, transportation and food-service systems.
headline: Springfield schools stay closed as severe cyberattack response continues
sourceName: NEPM via New Hampshire Public Radio

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: An attorney for Lindsay Clancy asked President Donald Trump to pardon his client Tuesday, days after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in the closely watched Plymouth County murder case.

Reuters reported that defense lawyer Kevin Reddington made the request during a television interview. Clancy was prosecuted in state court, however, and the Constitution gives presidents authority to pardon federal offenses, not state crimes. Any relief in a Massachusetts case would ordinarily have to come through the state’s own clemency process.

The mistrial followed jurors’ inability to reach a unanimous verdict. Prosecutors have not ruled out trying the case again, so the pardon appeal does not end the legal proceedings or prevent state authorities from moving forward.

The new request adds a political element to a case that has centered on criminal responsibility and mental health. It is also legally distinct from a formal clemency application. As of Tuesday evening, Reuters reported no indication that the White House had acted on the appeal. Court filings and statements from prosecutors will determine the case’s next steps.
dek: The request faces a basic jurisdictional obstacle: presidential pardon power covers federal offenses, while the Massachusetts case was brought under state law.
headline: Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer asks Trump for pardon after mistrial

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island entered primary day with a record 37,444 early in-person ballots cast, according to final figures reported Tuesday by Rhode Island Current from the Department of State.

The total, recorded as of 4 p.m., was more than twice the roughly 16,900 early in-person votes cast in the 2022 primary and more than triple the approximately 12,100 recorded in 2024. Rhode Island first offered early in-person voting in 2020 under pandemic-era rules that were later made permanent; just over 7,000 people used the option that year.

The surge came ahead of high-profile Democratic contests, including the gubernatorial rematch between Gov. Dan McKee and Helena Foulkes and the Providence mayoral primary between Brett Smiley and David Morales.

Early voting totals measure how people voted, not which candidates they supported, so the record does not by itself point to an outcome. It does show that a substantially larger share of the electorate chose to vote before Tuesday, a change that can affect campaign strategy, staffing and the pace at which election officials process ballots.
dek: More than 37,000 voters cast ballots before Election Day, more than doubling the state’s previous primary-year benchmark.
headline: Rhode Island primary sets record for early in-person voting

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A 17-year-old was charged with murder Tuesday in connection with the May shooting death of 20-year-old Joseph Ramos in Providence, city officials said.

According to WJAR, the teenager was arraigned in Family Court after Providence police detectives identified the youth during their investigation. Authorities did not release the defendant’s name because the person was a juvenile when the alleged crime occurred.

Officers found Ramos on Swift Street near Silver Spring Street shortly after 2:15 a.m. on May 11. He was taken to Rhode Island Hospital and later pronounced dead. Police said he had been riding a three-wheeled motor bike before the shooting.

Another defendant, Charles Ortiz, had previously been charged in the case. WJAR reported Tuesday that Ortiz entered a no-contest plea to conspiracy and drive-by shooting and that other charges, including murder, were dropped. The new juvenile charge is an allegation; guilt must be established in court. Police credited the Rhode Island attorney general’s office with assisting the investigation.
dek: Police say a 17-year-old was arraigned in Family Court Tuesday after an investigation into the May shooting death of the 20-year-old.
headline: Juvenile charged with murder in Providence killing of Joseph Ramos

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington won their parties’ New Hampshire gubernatorial primaries Tuesday, setting the matchup for November.

Citizens Count’s election results page listed both candidates as winners Tuesday evening. Ayotte entered the election seeking a second two-year term, while Warmington, a former member of the Executive Council, is making another run for governor after competing in the 2024 Democratic primary.

The results move the contest from intraparty campaigning to a general election likely to focus on housing costs, public education, energy prices, abortion policy and management of the state budget. Ayotte will run on her first term in office, while Warmington will argue for a change in direction after years of Republican control of the corner office.

Results posted on election night are preliminary until local returns are reviewed and the state completes its canvass. The nominations nevertheless clarify the top of New Hampshire’s state ballot and give both campaigns less than two months to consolidate supporters and reach independent voters.
dek: The incumbent Republican governor and former Democratic Executive Councilor advance to the November general election.
headline: Ayotte and Warmington win New Hampshire governor primaries

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The U.S. military said Tuesday that it destroyed five Iranian crude-oil tankers after Iran’s Revolutionary Guard tried twice to strike an American warship with ballistic missiles over the previous two days.

U.S. Central Command announced the action in a social media post, according to the Associated Press. The military described the tanker strikes as a response to the attempted attacks on the warship. The AP did not immediately report the names of the vessels, their locations or independent confirmation of the damage.

The exchange marks a new escalation in more than six months of conflict between Washington and Tehran. It also adds uncertainty around energy shipping at a time when attacks on Saudi facilities and disruptions near major Gulf export routes have already pushed oil prices higher.

Because the situation is developing, early military claims may change as more information becomes available. The immediate questions include whether there were casualties, how Iran will respond and whether commercial traffic faces new restrictions. Shipping notices and statements from regional governments will be critical to verifying the wider impact.
dek: Central Command said the strikes answered two attempted ballistic-missile attacks on a U.S. warship over two days.
headline: U.S. says it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers after warship attacks

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The U.S. government accused six Chinese artificial-intelligence companies Tuesday of maliciously copying American technology through large-scale model distillation, escalating a dispute over how advanced AI systems are built and protected.

Reuters reported that officials named DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba among the companies accused of using outputs from models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceX. Distillation is a common technical approach in which a smaller model learns from the responses of a larger one, but providers can restrict automated extraction or uses that violate their terms.

U.S. officials argued that the activity could speed Chinese research and strengthen military or cyber capabilities. The allegations arrived ahead of planned U.S.-China discussions on AI safety and a meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

The claims are government allegations, not a court finding. Reuters said the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond. The next issue is whether the administration follows the statement with export controls, sanctions or enforcement against companies and intermediaries, steps that could further split the global AI supply chain.
dek: Officials say companies including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba used American model outputs at scale to accelerate their own systems.
headline: U.S. accuses six Chinese AI firms of malicious model copying

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Meta launched a new artificial-intelligence agent called Muse in the United States on Tuesday, giving users a tool designed to send email, book travel, make payments and carry out other tasks across connected apps.

Reuters reported that Muse is initially available through a standalone app and WhatsApp. Users choose which services to connect and can revoke access, while each agent runs in a separate cloud-based virtual machine so it can continue working in the background.

The launch raises the stakes for agent security because the system can reach sensitive categories including calendars, shopping, health information and smart-home controls. Reuters reported that Meta delayed the release for additional safeguards after internal testing identified reliability and privacy problems, including unintended uploads and access concerns.

Meta says the product meets its safety and privacy standards, while acknowledging that errors remain possible. The rollout will test whether consumers are willing to grant an AI assistant broad access in exchange for convenience. Clear permission prompts, activity logs and rapid revocation will matter as much as the range of tasks the agent can complete.
dek: The new assistant can work across connected services in the background, putting privacy and security controls at the center of its rollout.
headline: Meta launches Muse AI agent with email, payment and app access

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: GE Aerospace agreed to acquire Consolidated Precision Products for $11.75 billion, a major bet that owning more of its supply chain will help relieve shortages constraining aircraft-engine production.

Reuters reported that CPP makes precision castings used in GE’s LEAP and GEnx engines as well as other commercial and defense programs. Castings have been a persistent bottleneck for engine manufacturers as airlines and aircraft makers press for faster deliveries.

GE plans to finance the purchase with $7 billion in cash and additional debt. The company expects the transaction to close in the second half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions. It is GE Aerospace’s largest acquisition since becoming an independent company in 2024.

For investors, the deal trades a large upfront cost for greater control over a strategically important supplier. It could improve production reliability if integration goes well, but it also brings execution risk and may draw scrutiny because CPP supplies other engine makers, including GE competitors. The announced value and timeline are deal terms, not live market prices.
dek: The planned acquisition would bring a critical engine-parts supplier in-house as manufacturers work through persistent production bottlenecks.
headline: GE Aerospace to buy castings supplier CPP for $11.75 billion

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Financial-technology company Chime agreed Tuesday to acquire nationally chartered Stride Bank for $590 million, a move intended to bring core banking infrastructure under Chime’s direct control.

Reuters reported that the transaction would give Chime access to Stride’s national charter and capabilities as it expands lending and other financial products. Chime has historically relied on partner banks to hold customer deposits and provide regulated banking services behind its app.

Investors pushed Chime shares higher after the announcement, Reuters said, reflecting optimism that the structure could improve economics and reduce dependence on outside institutions. The acquisition still requires regulatory approval, and ownership of a bank would also subject Chime to direct supervision, capital requirements and compliance obligations.

The deal is significant beyond its $590 million price tag because it reflects a broader shift among large fintech companies toward tighter control of regulated infrastructure. Closing terms and the exact timing could change during review. Any share move cited in connection with the announcement reflects reported trading at that time, not a live quote.
dek: The fintech company is seeking a national bank charter and more control over the infrastructure behind its accounts and lending expansion.
headline: Chime agrees to buy Stride Bank for $590 million

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: President Donald Trump posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom Tuesday to Welles Crowther, the Boston College graduate remembered as the “Man in the Red Bandana” for rescuing people at the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.

Crowther, an equities trader and volunteer firefighter, repeatedly guided people from the South Tower’s upper floors toward safety before the building collapsed. Survivors later connected their unknown rescuer to Crowther through the red bandana he carried, a habit that became central to his legacy.
WHDH reported that Crowther is credited with helping save as many as 18 people. His mother, Alison Crowther, accepted the honor and said it would be treasured by the family for generations.

The award comes days before the 25th anniversary of the attacks and renews attention on a story with deep New England ties. Boston College has memorialized Crowther through an annual 5K and other campus traditions. The medal, the nation’s highest civilian honor, recognizes his courage and the lives he helped save.
dek: The Boston College graduate and volunteer firefighter was honored posthumously for helping people escape the World Trade Center on Sept. 11.
headline: ‘Man in the Red Bandana’ Welles Crowther awarded Medal of Freedom

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The first trailer for M. Night Shyamalan’s “Remain” arrived Tuesday, offering audiences an early look at the supernatural romantic thriller filmed around Rhode Island.

Entertainment Weekly reported that Jake Gyllenhaal plays a reclusive architect who meets a mysterious woman, portrayed by Phoebe Dynevor, after moving to a coastal community. The preview begins with the tone of a romance before shifting toward the suspense associated with Shyamalan’s films.

The project grew from a story Shyamalan developed with novelist Nicholas Sparks. Shyamalan wrote and directed the screen version, while Sparks produced a novel based on the same idea. The supporting cast includes Ashley Walters, Julie Hagerty and Jay O. Sanders.

For Rhode Island, the trailer is also a showcase for a production that used locations around the state during filming, including coastal communities and Providence-area sites. Warner Bros. has scheduled the movie for theatrical release on Feb. 5, 2027. The trailer gives local viewers their first chance to see how familiar settings were transformed for the finished film.
dek: M. Night Shyamalan’s supernatural romance, filmed around the Ocean State, pairs Jake Gyllenhaal and Phoebe Dynevor ahead of a February release.
headline: First ‘Remain’ trailer brings Rhode Island-shot thriller into view

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Anthony DiLorenzo won the Republican primary Tuesday for New Hampshire’s open 1st Congressional District seat, advancing to the November election in one of the state’s most competitive federal races.

The Associated Press called the race for DiLorenzo, a businessman making his first run for office. He received President Donald Trump’s endorsement during a crowded Republican contest that also included Brian Cole, Hollie Noveletsky and other candidates.

The seat is open because Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas ran for U.S. Senate rather than seeking another House term. The district includes Manchester, much of the Seacoast and communities extending into the Lakes Region, making it geographically and politically varied.

The Democratic primary had not been called in the AP report used for this update. Election-night totals remain unofficial until New Hampshire completes its canvass, but the Republican result gives DiLorenzo a short general-election runway before Nov. 3. The race will determine who succeeds Pappas in the closely watched district.
dek: The Trump-backed businessman advances in the race to replace Rep. Chris Pappas in the 1st Congressional District.
headline: Anthony DiLorenzo wins GOP primary for open New Hampshire House seat

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Democratic Rep. Maggie Goodlander and Republican Lily Tang Williams won their respective primaries Tuesday in New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District, setting up a rematch of the 2024 general election.

New Hampshire Public Radio reported that both candidates won comfortably. Goodlander defeated state Rep. Paige Beauchemin in the Democratic primary, while Williams emerged from the Republican field to secure another nomination.

Goodlander won the open seat in 2024 and is seeking a second term. Williams was the Republican nominee in that election. The district covers western and northern New Hampshire and includes Nashua, Concord and many rural communities.

The general election will take place Nov. 3. The matchup adds another federal race to a busy New Hampshire ballot that also includes an open U.S. Senate seat and an open 1st Congressional District seat. Tuesday night’s returns are preliminary until election officials complete the canvass, but the primary results establish the major-party field in the 2nd District.
dek: The incumbent Democrat and Republican challenger will meet again after facing each other in the district’s 2024 general election.
headline: Goodlander and Williams win New Hampshire 2nd District primaries

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A car struck a utility pole and a parked food truck on Route 138 in Taunton Tuesday afternoon, snapping the pole and leaving the vehicle on its side, according to witnesses and video from the scene.
WJAR reported that bystanders rushed to help the driver out of the car. The driver appeared disoriented and was taken to a hospital; authorities had not released an updated condition Tuesday evening.

The collision damaged Hetty’s Sweets Bakery and Savory Foods, a food truck that had opened only a week earlier. A co-owner told the station the business represented the owners’ life savings. No customers or workers were reported injured in the truck.

Neighbors said speeding has been a recurring concern along that section of Route 138, though police had not said what caused this crash. Investigators had not announced charges. The utility damage and the food truck’s losses were still being assessed, making the incident a developing local story rather than a final account.
dek: Witnesses helped the driver after a car hit a pole and the week-old Hetty’s Sweets Bakery and Savory Foods truck on Route 138.
headline: Taunton crash snaps utility pole and damages new food truck

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A property dispute in Swansea is creating uncertainty for a Toys for Tots operation that has used facilities at the Nike Site Road baseball field to collect and store donations for six years.

The program’s coordinator for Bristol County and North Plymouth County told WJAR that the drive could be jeopardized by a conflict between the town and the Swansea Independent Baseball League, which originally provided access to the site.

Town officials have asked Toys for Tots to sign a facility-use agreement before entering the property this year. Coordinator Kimberly Johnson said the standard agreement could be read as recognizing the town as the sole controller of the site, potentially compromising the charity’s neutrality in the local dispute.

The disagreement has not yet canceled the holiday drive, and the parties could still revise the agreement or identify another location. The immediate issue is securing reliable space before donations and distribution accelerate. Any final arrangement will need to preserve the charity’s access while avoiding a position on who controls the baseball complex.
dek: The Bristol and North Plymouth counties coordinator says an access agreement could pull the charity into a dispute over a baseball complex.
headline: Swansea property dispute puts local Toys for Tots drive in doubt

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Hasbro says it is looking to formally establish its new Boston headquarters in January, one year after the toy and game company announced it would move from Pawtucket to the Seaport District.

WJAR reported that there was no visible Hasbro presence Tuesday at the planned 265,000-square-foot Summer Street location. The company previously said about 700 full-time employees would relocate from Rhode Island.

Pawtucket Mayor Don Grebien told the station that employees are now receiving transfer dates or severance information and that some moves could begin in November. He said city officials were learning details through employees rather than direct communication from the company.

Hasbro traces its roots to Providence in the 1920s and has spent more than a century in Rhode Island, so the move carries economic and civic significance beyond the office lease. Pawtucket is considering possible future uses for the Newport Avenue property, including housing or industrial space. The January target remains a company timeline and could change as construction and transfers proceed.
dek: One year after announcing the relocation, the company says its Seaport headquarters is expected to open in January while employee moves may begin sooner.
headline: Hasbro targets January for Boston headquarters as Pawtucket exit nears

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Johnston parents rallied outside Town Hall ahead of a school committee meeting, saying students continue to face long rides, delays and limited communication under the district’s new bus provider.

WJAR reported that families have raised concerns about Zum since the school year began. District and company officials have said service is improving, but parents at the rally said the changes have not gone far enough.

Some middle-school students said they must wake up especially early because their buses first transport high-school students. Other students have arrived well before class and waited in school gymnasiums for as long as an hour after the district separated routes serving two elementary schools.

The dispute is now about more than isolated late buses: families want clear responsibility, dependable pickup times and direct updates when routes change. The school committee and provider have not announced a final resolution. Performance over the coming days will show whether route adjustments reduce delays or whether Johnston needs a broader transportation plan.
dek: Families say communication and routing problems persist weeks after the district began working with a new transportation provider.
headline: Johnston parents rally as school-bus delays and long rides continue

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A construction worker sustained a minor injury Tuesday when the roof framework of a building under construction collapsed in Burrillville, according to local authorities.

Burrillville police said the collapse happened at about 12:55 p.m. near Douglas Pike and Ironmine Road. WJAR reported that one worker was hurt; officials did not report additional injuries or identify the worker.

The town’s building inspector is expected to assess the site as authorities investigate why the framing failed. Officials had not released the building’s intended use, the name of the contractor or details about how many people were present when the structure came down.

The reported injury was minor, but a structural collapse can require the area to remain secured until inspectors determine whether other portions are stable. The cause remains unknown, and no violation or fault has been assigned. Updates from the town, police and building inspector will determine whether construction can resume and whether additional safety review is needed.
dek: Town officials are investigating after roof framing collapsed near Douglas Pike and Ironmine Road Tuesday afternoon.
headline: Worker injured in Burrillville construction-site roof collapse

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: All five people killed when an Amazon cargo jet ran off a runway at Miami International Airport were inside a van used by aircraft cleaners, investigators said Tuesday.

The Associated Press reported that the flight was operated by North Carolina-based carrier 21 Air. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 began service as a passenger jet and was converted for cargo use in 2015, according to flight-tracking data cited by the AP.

Two of the airport’s four runways remained closed while National Transportation Safety Board investigators documented the wreckage and gathered evidence. More than 225 flights were canceled Sunday and Monday, with hundreds of additional delays, airport officials said.

The latest information clarifies where the victims were when the crash occurred but does not establish why the aircraft left the runway. The NTSB investigation will examine the plane, crew actions, weather, airport conditions and available recordings before reaching conclusions. Officials said runways would reopen after investigators completed necessary work at the scene.
dek: Investigators say the victims were inside a plane-cleaning vehicle when a Boeing 767 ran off the runway at Miami International Airport.
headline: Five killed in Miami cargo-jet crash were in ground-crew van

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Boston Logan International Airport has deployed a multilingual AI-powered hologram named Amelia at nine locations across its four terminals, giving travelers another way to ask for directions and local information.

WHDH reported that Amelia can guide passengers around the airport and identify about 400 points of interest in Boston. The system is intended to remain available during overnight and other hours when fewer staff members may be present.

Proto Hologram, the company behind the system, describes it as a first-of-its-kind airport deployment. Related technology is already used at the Patriots Hall of Fame at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough.

The rollout will test whether an AI avatar can reduce routine wayfinding pressure without confusing travelers who need human help. Airports are complex, frequently changing environments, so accuracy about gates, ground transportation and accessibility services will be essential. The report did not specify the project’s cost, data-retention rules or whether Amelia connects directly to live flight systems. Those details will shape how useful and trustworthy the service becomes.
dek: The multilingual digital assistant is designed to help travelers navigate terminals and find hundreds of Boston destinations, including after staffed hours.
headline: Logan Airport deploys ‘Amelia’ AI holograms at nine locations

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: ASML plans to work with major chipmakers on larger masks for its newest High-NA extreme-ultraviolet lithography tools, aiming to make the systems suitable for large data-center processors.

Reuters reported that widely used EUV machines can print chips up to about 800 square millimeters. High-NA tools can create finer features, but their smaller masks currently limit the size of chips they can produce.

ASML said a larger mask format could remove that constraint and expand adoption beyond Intel, which already uses the new tools for some production. TSMC plans High-NA use in advanced-node high-volume manufacturing from 2030, while Samsung and SK Hynix are targeting memory production earlier.

The timetable is long: ASML expects a pilot line around 2031 and technology ready for high-volume production by 2033. Chief Technology Officer Marco Pieters told Reuters the change could raise system productivity by 40%. Those are company plans, not guaranteed manufacturing outcomes, and success will require equipment makers, chip foundries and mask suppliers to align on a new standard.
dek: The chip-equipment maker says an industry consortium could adapt its most advanced lithography systems for today’s largest AI processors.
headline: ASML plans larger masks for High-NA tools and data-center chips

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Canadian oil producers Tamarack Valley and Headwater Exploration agreed to merge in an all-stock transaction valued at C$10 billion, or about $7.25 billion, the companies said Tuesday.

Reuters reported that Headwater investors would receive one Tamarack share for each share held. Existing Tamarack shareholders would own 66.5% of the combined company, while Headwater shareholders would hold 33.5%.

The deal would combine major positions in Alberta’s Clearwater Formation and is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to approvals. Tamarack also plans to raise its quarterly dividend 20% to C$0.06 a share and spin non-core assets into a separate listed company.

Reuters reported that Tamarack shares gained more than 4% and Headwater nearly 2% after the announcement. Those moves reflect trading at the time of the report, not live prices. Investors will now weigh expected scale and pipeline access against integration risk, commodity-price exposure and the possibility that transaction terms or timing change before closing.
dek: The all-stock transaction would create the largest publicly traded producer focused on Alberta’s Clearwater Formation.
headline: Tamarack and Headwater agree to $7.25 billion oil merger

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Verizon signed a multibillion-dollar agreement with Corning for high-density optical fiber and connectivity products, extending a supplier relationship that has lasted about three decades.

Reuters reported that Corning will provide more than 80 million miles of fiber between 2027 and 2032. Verizon said the equipment will support broadband expansion for homes and businesses and add capacity for large AI computing customers that need fast, low-latency connections.

The companies described the agreement as multibillion-dollar but did not disclose exact financial terms. That limits how precisely investors can estimate revenue timing, margins or capital requirements from the announcement alone.

The deal illustrates how AI spending is expanding beyond processors and data centers into the networks connecting them. For Corning, it provides a long-duration customer commitment; for Verizon, it secures supply for planned construction. The ultimate financial effect will depend on deployment pace, customer demand and execution over several years. No stock price in this report should be treated as a live quote.
dek: Corning will supply more than 80 million miles of high-density optical fiber from 2027 through 2032 for broadband and AI infrastructure.
headline: Verizon signs multibillion-dollar fiber deal with Corning

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Boston Bruins signed center Fraser Minten to a seven-year, $50.4 million contract extension Tuesday, locking up the 22-year-old through the 2033-34 season.

The Associated Press reported that the deal carries an average annual value and salary-cap hit of $7.2 million. Minten will first complete the final year of his rookie contract, which pays a base salary of $850,000 this season.

Boston acquired Minten from Toronto in March 2025 in the trade that sent defenseman Brandon Carlo to the Maple Leafs. Minten then played all 82 games last season, recording career highs of 17 goals and 18 assists. His 35 points were the most by a Bruins rookie since 2017-18, and his plus-21 rating led NHL rookies.

The extension gives Boston a younger long-term piece alongside established stars David Pastrnak and Charlie McAvoy. It also shifts performance risk to the club: the contract becomes especially valuable if Minten continues developing, but costly if his production stalls. The announced value is the full contract total, not a one-season salary.
dek: The 22-year-old center is under contract through 2033-34 after producing 35 points in his first full season with Boston.
headline: Bruins sign Fraser Minten to seven-year, $50.4 million extension

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Yolanda Celucci, a longtime Boston fashion designer and philanthropist known across the region’s style and charitable communities, has died at age 91.

WHDH reported that Celucci worked with celebrities, designers and presidents during a career that made her a prominent figure in Boston fashion. She also used that visibility to support charitable fundraising.

Through the Waltham Lions Club, Celucci helped raise millions of dollars for charity, according to the station. That work connected her fashion career with causes serving people in Greater Boston and beyond.

The report did not state a cause of death or provide funeral arrangements. Celucci is survived by a daughter, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Her legacy rests in both the public events and designs that shaped Boston’s fashion scene and the fundraising relationships she built over decades. Additional details about memorial services may be released by her family or community organizations. Her death closes a notable chapter in the region’s creative and civic life.
dek: A prominent figure in the region’s fashion community, Celucci also helped raise millions of dollars for charity through the Waltham Lions Club.
headline: Boston fashion designer and philanthropist Yolanda Celucci dies at 91
